scope: Twenty main-paper sources with distinct roles. Technical claims use primary papers or standards. The original eighteen were checked on 15 and 19 November; ZDNS was added on 20 November and Paris traceroute on 23 November 2026. Lu et al. (2019) remains supplemental-only in RELATED_BENCHMARKS.md. This project is a replication and measurement audit, not a new protocol or first global measurement.

references.title: An Empirical Study of the Cost of DNS-over-HTTPS
references.apa: Böttger, T., Cuadrado, F., Antichi, G., Fernandes, E. L., Tyson, G., Castro, I., & Uhlig, S. (2019). An empirical study of the cost of DNS-over-HTTPS. In Proceedings of the Internet Measurement Conference (pp. 15–21). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3355369.3355575

claims.claim: Persistent connections amortize setup overhead, while larger DNS costs need not translate directly to larger page-load costs.
claims.relation: Motivates separate fresh/established treatments and separate lookup versus browser outcomes.
claims.boundary: One university vantage point and historical software; its numerical effects are not predictions for this dataset.

references.metadata_note: Proceedings pp. 15–21 verified against authors' institutional publication records; full-text preprint uses its own PDF pagination.

references.title: Comparing the Effects of DNS, DoT, and DoH on Web Performance
references.apa: Hounsel, A., Borgolte, K., Schmitt, P., Holland, J., & Feamster, N. (2020). Comparing the effects of DNS, DoT, and DoH on web performance. In Proceedings of The Web Conference 2020 (pp. 562–572). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3366423.3380139

claims.claim: DNS response-time rankings and browser page-load rankings can differ; network conditions and retransmission behavior matter.
claims.relation: Supports treating lookup latency and load-event time as separate outcomes, with actual browser measurement.
claims.boundary: Their native Firefox/global-cloud experiment is substantially broader than our intercepted-content fixture.

references.metadata_note: Author-hosted publication page and author CV verify final venue/year and pp. 562–572; preprint originated in 2019 but publication year is 2020.

references.title: Can Encrypted DNS Be Fast?
references.apa: Hounsel, A., Schmitt, P., Borgolte, K., & Feamster, N. (2021). Can encrypted DNS be fast? In O. Hohlfeld, A. Lutu, & D. Levin (Eds.), Passive and active measurement (pp. 444–459). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-72582-2_26

claims.claim: Connection setup and query response time are separate costs, and no resolver/protocol combination performs best for every measured client.
claims.relation: Motivates verified connection-state treatments and conditional, provider-specific interpretation.
claims.boundary: 2,693 analyzed US home-network devices; no browser page-load measurements. This does not establish our short-window sign changes' cause.

references.metadata_note: Use the final publisher count 2,693; one author webpage has a discrepant older count.

references.title: Measuring DNS-over-HTTPS Performance Around the World
references.apa: Chhabra, R., Murley, P., Kumar, D., Bailey, M., & Wang, G. (2021). Measuring DNS-over-HTTPS performance around the world. In Proceedings of the 21st ACM Internet Measurement Conference (pp. 351–365). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3487552.3487849

claims.claim: The worldwide comparison uses clients' default resolver baseline, unique names under a controlled authoritative zone, and explicit connection-reuse distinctions.
claims.locator: Sections 3.1 and 3.4, printed pp. 353 and 355; Section 5 terminology, p. 357; cache limitation in Section 7, p. 362
claims.relation: Required anchor; we adapt the connection distinction while using fixed providers and openly unknown recursive-cache state.
claims.boundary: Our data do not replicate their worldwide coverage, cache-miss control or default-resolver estimand.

references.title: Cache Me If You Can: Effects of DNS Time-to-Live
references.apa: Moura, G. C. M., Heidemann, J., Schmidt, R. de O., & Hardaker, W. (2019). Cache me if you can: Effects of DNS time-to-live. In Proceedings of the Internet Measurement Conference (pp. 101–115). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3355369.3355568

claims.claim: TTL effects emerge from distributed caches, differing record sources and resolver behavior, and materially affect observed DNS latency.
claims.relation: Explains why direct queries and prewarming do not prove a globally fixed recursive-cache state; TTLs remain diagnostics.
claims.boundary: Do not attribute our time-window changes to cache expiration without authoritative/cache-hit evidence.

references.title: Anycast Latency: How Many Sites Are Enough?
references.apa: de Oliveira Schmidt, R., Heidemann, J., & Kuipers, J. H. (2017). Anycast latency: How many sites are enough? In M. A. Kaafar, S. Uhlig, & J. Amann (Eds.), Passive and active measurement (pp. 188–200). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-54328-4_14

claims.claim: An anycast IP is announced from multiple physical sites; routing policies affect client-to-site mapping and latency.
claims.locator: Abstract and Section 1, author PDF pp. 1–2; publisher abstract
claims.relation: Pinning provider IP and SNI controls destination service identity, without proving identical physical site or backend cache.
claims.boundary: Their study concerns four root services. It does not demonstrate a route or site change in our recursive-resolver trials.

references.metadata_note: Publisher citation styles the family name de Oliveira Schmidt; author paper often abbreviates it Ricardo de O. Schmidt. Cite consistently.

references.title: DNS Privacy with Speed? Evaluating DNS over QUIC and Its Impact on Web Performance
references.apa: Kosek, M., Schumann, L., Marx, R., Doan, T. V., & Bajpai, V. (2022). DNS privacy with speed? Evaluating DNS over QUIC and its impact on web performance. In Proceedings of the 22nd ACM Internet Measurement Conference (pp. 44–50). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3517745.3561445

claims.claim: Distributed measurements distinguish handshake from resolution time and evaluate DoQ against HTTP/2 DoH, with session resumption explicitly recorded.
claims.locator: Sections 2–3.2, author PDF pp. 2–5; especially Section 3, p. 3
claims.relation: Supports treating HTTP version, resumption and transport as experimental conditions, rather than a single generic encrypted-DNS cost.
claims.boundary: DoQ and resumed TLS are outside our non-resumed HTTP/2 treatments; do not import their speedups into our results.

references.title: Effects of Secured DNS Transport on Resolver Performance
references.apa: Le Louët, E., Blin, A., Sopena, J., Haddadou, K., & Amaou, A. (2024). Effects of secured DNS transport on resolver performance. ITU Journal on Future and Evolving Technologies, 5(1), 47–61. https://doi.org/10.52953/NUXL5710

claims.claim: Resolver resource cost can be separated into connection establishment, connection upkeep and message processing; client connection behavior affects server load.
claims.relation: Provides the computer-architecture connection while showing that elapsed lookup latency is not a CPU-cycle, memory or energy measurement.
claims.boundary: Their controlled server benchmarks and throughput costs cannot be estimated from our client-side wall-clock delays.

references.metadata_note: ITU landing metadata and article byline print Ahmed Amaou, while the author biography on p. 61 prints Ahmed Amamou. The APA string preserves the published byline/metadata. Do not silently claim these spellings are identical.

references.title: On Cross-Layer Interactions of QUIC, Encrypted DNS and HTTP/3: Design, Evaluation, and Dataset
references.apa: Sengupta, J., Kosek, M., Fries, J., Ferlin-Reiter, S., & Bajpai, V. (2024). On cross-layer interactions of QUIC, encrypted DNS and HTTP/3: Design, evaluation, and dataset. IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management, 21(3), 2992–3007. https://doi.org/10.1109/TNSM.2024.3383787

claims.claim: DNS and content-transport handshakes interact on the page-loading path; coalescing DoQ and HTTP/3 changes the setup structure.
claims.locator: Abstract, Section I and Figure 1, author PDF pp. 1–2
claims.relation: Explains why a DNS-gated local-content fixture cannot estimate real content-transport, connection-coalescing or CDN effects.
claims.boundary: Do not describe their cross-layer gains as a property measured by our HTTP/2-only fixture.

references.metadata_note: Final journal byline has five authors. Earlier arXiv metadata includes a different author list; use the final journal list above. Publisher issue metadata verifies pp. 2992–3007.

references.title: The Future of DNS Privacy: A Comparison of DNS over QUIC and DNS over HTTP/3
references.apa: Bielefeld, P., Hoffmann, F., Sassalla, S., ververis, v., & Bajpai, V. (2026). The future of DNS privacy: A comparison of DNS over QUIC and DNS over HTTP/3. In S. Ferlin-Reiter, R. Fontugne, & J. Ullrich (Eds.), Passive and active measurement (pp. 202–228). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-18268-5_10

claims.claim: A current study combines resolver feature probing with browser experiments; performance depends on supported resumption/0-RTT behavior, and DNS delay does not necessarily become equivalent page-load delay.
claims.locator: Section 3.1–3.4, author PDF pp. 10–12; Sections 4–6 and conclusion, pp. 16–23
claims.relation: Makes the literature current and confines our observations to h2 without resumption, while supporting separate application measurements.
claims.boundary: Their DoQ/DoH3 and Firefox-proxy results are not interchangeable with our HTTP/2 local-content fixture.

references.metadata_note: Publisher first online 10 March 2026, LNCS 16477. Publisher spells Sassalla; the author manuscript byline spells Sasalla. Use the publisher's spelling and preserve ververis's preferred lowercase form.

references.title: Domain Names—Implementation and Specification
references.apa: Mockapetris, P. (1987). Domain names—Implementation and specification (RFC 1035). RFC Editor. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC1035

claims.claim: DNS message structure, UDP port 53 transport and TTL-governed record caching are separately specified.
claims.relation: Basis for matching wire-format A queries and independently validating stored responses.
claims.boundary: Bypassing the OS resolver does not remove recursive caching; that is an inference from the separate cache layers.

references.title: DNS Queries over HTTPS (DoH)
references.apa: Hoffman, P., & McManus, P. (2018). DNS queries over HTTPS (DoH) (RFC 8484). RFC Editor. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC8484

claims.claim: DoH maps DNS messages to HTTP exchanges; HTTP/2 is recommended, HTTP and DNS caches interact, and transport security is distinct from DNSSEC.
claims.relation: Protocol definition, wire-format POST validation and precise privacy framing.
claims.boundary: DoH protects the client-resolver channel, not anonymity from the resolver; no privacy effectiveness was tested.

references.title: HTTP/2
references.apa: Thomson, M., & Benfield, C. (Eds.). (2022). HTTP/2 (RFC 9113). RFC Editor. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC9113

claims.claim: HTTP/2 provides streams, field compression and connection management over TCP.
claims.relation: Basis for h2 negotiation and one shared connection across a page's concurrent hostname gates.
claims.boundary: Multiplexed streams do not make HTTP/2 equivalent to QUIC or eliminate all TCP-level blocking.

references.title: DNS over Dedicated QUIC Connections
references.apa: Huitema, C., Dickinson, S., & Mankin, A. (2022). DNS over dedicated QUIC connections (RFC 9250). RFC Editor. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC9250

claims.claim: DoQ is a dedicated DNS mapping over QUIC with resumption, 0-RTT and persistent-connection considerations.
claims.relation: Defines an unmeasured transport boundary and a concrete future comparison.
claims.boundary: A standards mechanism is not empirical proof of a universal speed advantage.

references.title: HTTP/3
references.apa: Bishop, M. (Ed.). (2022). HTTP/3 (RFC 9114). RFC Editor. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC9114

claims.claim: HTTP/3 maps HTTP onto QUIC, with transport and stream-delivery behavior distinct from TCP-based HTTP/2.
claims.relation: Explains why measured h2 DoH overhead cannot be extrapolated to DoH3.
claims.boundary: Dedicated DoQ and DoH over HTTP/3 remain different protocol mappings.

references.title: Navigation Timing Level 2
references.apa: Weiss, Y., & Rosenthal, N. (Eds.). (2026, November 2). Navigation timing level 2 (W3C Working Draft). World Wide Web Consortium. https://www.w3.org/TR/2026/WD-navigation-timing-2-20261102/

claims.claim: A navigation entry starts at zero and its duration ends at loadEventEnd, after load-event handling.
claims.relation: Defines the fixture's browser metric precisely.
claims.boundary: A load event is not visual completeness, interactivity, or completion of all future lazy-loaded content.

references.title: Bootstrapping Clustered Data
references.apa: Field, C. A., & Welsh, A. H. (2007). Bootstrapping clustered data. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), 69(3), 369–390. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2007.00593.x

claims.claim: Bootstrap validity depends on the dependence structure and model used for clustered observations.
claims.relation: Motivates preserving matched blocks and qualifying conditional uncertainty estimates.
claims.boundary: Does not validate this exact median bootstrap or well-calibrated population inference from three short windows; those cautions are our methodological judgment.

references.title: The Dagstuhl Beginners Guide to Reproducibility for Experimental Networking Research
references.source_type: Primary expert editorial and methodological guide; explicitly not peer reviewed
references.apa: Bajpai, V., Brunstrom, A., Feldmann, A., Kellerer, W., Pras, A., Schulzrinne, H., Smaragdakis, G., Wählisch, M., & Wehrle, K. (2019). The Dagstuhl beginners guide to reproducibility for experimental networking research. ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review, 49(1), 24–30. https://doi.org/10.1145/3314212.3314217

claims.claim: Operational Internet measurements require repeated observations, documented metadata, raw-data preservation, validated tooling and explicit time/vantage-point scope.
claims.relation: Supports machine-readable raw data, seeds, validation, timestamps and a repeatable analysis package.
claims.boundary: Code/data availability improves inspectability; it does not guarantee future Internet timings reproduce numerically. This is not a peer-reviewed empirical DNS study.

references.title: ZDNS: A Fast DNS Toolkit for Internet Measurement
references.apa: Izhikevich, L., Akiwate, G., Berger, B., Drakontaidis, S., Ascheman, A., Pearce, P., Adrian, D., & Durumeric, Z. (2022). ZDNS: A fast DNS toolkit for internet measurement. In Proceedings of the 22nd ACM Internet Measurement Conference (pp. 33–43). Association for Computing Machinery. https://doi.org/10.1145/3517745.3561434

claims.claim: ZDNS uses long-lived UDP sockets to avoid per-lookup socket creation and teardown work.
claims.locator: Section 3.4 Performance Optimizations, UDP Socket Reuse, author PDF p. 3
claims.relation: Motivates a reusable UDP sensitivity treatment and explicit resource-readiness timing boundaries in this benchmark.
claims.boundary: The paper evaluates a high-throughput Internet measurement toolkit; it does not supply a per-query latency correction for this client, operating system or workload.

references.metadata_note: Title, author order, year and DOI verified in the original author-hosted paper on 20 November 2026. The IMC publication is 2022; the later arXiv upload is 2023. Proceedings pages 33–43; author PDF has separate pagination.

references.title: Avoiding traceroute anomalies with Paris traceroute
references.apa: Augustin, B., Cuvellier, X., Orgogozo, B., Viger, F., Friedman, T., Latapy, M., Magnien, C., & Teixeira, R. (2006). Avoiding traceroute anomalies with Paris traceroute. claims.claim: Per-flow load balancing can depend on transport ports, so separate flows can follow different paths.
claims.locator: Section 2.1, conference PDF pp. 1–2; implementation discussion in Section 2.2, p. 3
claims.relation: Motivates checking sensitivity across persistent UDP sockets and HTTP/2 connections.
